summary:
This run covered 13 evals (24 iterations), 2 of which were negative-trigger evals marked skipped ("should_trigger: false") and so contribute no comparative data beyond a passing trigger check. Of the remaining 11 evals, with_skill produced a scorable result in all 11, while without_skill only produced a scorable result (non-null expected_output/assertions/metrics) in 6 of the 11 — for the other 5 evals (kb-vector-index-deleted, invocation-log-destination-unprotected, direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, bc-iam-boundary) without_skill's data is simply absent (null), so no comparison could be made there; this should be read as missing data, not as a failure for without_skill.

Where both variants have data, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output in 6/6 of those evals (all high confidence), while without_skill met expected output in only 3/6 (access-denied-iam-vs-scp, legacy-model-in-use, bc-req-schema, bc-ip-required partially — specifically it failed expected_output on stale-rag-ingestion-and-chunking, kb-never-synced, and kb-role-cannot-read-bucket). Assertion-level pass rates follow the same direction: with_skill scored 100% or near-100% assertions on every eval with data, while without_skill's assertion pass rates were lower across the board (e.g., 80% vs 100% on access-denied-iam-vs-scp, 40% vs 80% on stale-rag-ingestion, 20% vs 100% on kb-never-synced, 0% vs 100% on kb-role-cannot-read-bucket, 40% vs 100% on legacy-model-in-use, 50% vs 83% on bc-req-schema, 83% vs 100% on bc-ip-required).

Looking at individual assertions rather than aggregates is informative: several assertions passed for both variants (e.g., "no raw account ID exposed" on bc-ip-required and bc-req-schema, hybrid-search recommendation on stale-rag-ingestion, several on legacy-model and access-denied evals) — these aren't differentiating. One assertion ("report chunk counts but not reproduce chunk content" in stale-rag-ingestion) failed for both variants, suggesting that specific behavior needs work regardless of variant. Most other assertions that differ follow the with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, with no case found where without_skill passed an assertion that with_skill failed. One assertion (on legacy-model-in-use, about raising LLM-INV-003) was tagged with a low avg_confidence for without_skill's failing judgment, so that specific finding is weaker evidence than the high-confidence majority.

Where head-to-head quality comparisons were run (4 of the 11 non-skipped evals; the rest were skipped as pairs because one side lacked data), results were mixed: without_skill was favored on accuracy/actionability/completeness for access-denied-iam-vs-scp and bc-req-schema, while with_skill was favored for legacy-model-in-use and (narrowly, 2-1) for bc-ip-required. All these quality judgments carry only medium confidence, so they should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper where comparable (e.g., 8s/$0.07 vs 24s/$0.20 on access-denied-iam-vs-scp; 26s/$0.22 vs 57s/$0.48 on stale-rag-ingestion; 18s vs 59s on legacy-model-in-use), with one exception where without_skill was slower and more expensive (bc-ip-required: 2m33s/$1.28 vs with_skill's 1m15s/$0.63). Context-window utilization was also consistently lower for without_skill across evals.

No output_consistency data (repeated-run variability) was available for either variant in any eval — this dimension is entirely absent from the results.

Overall, the picture is one of a tradeoff with an asymmetry in available data: with_skill has complete data across all evals and shows stronger expected-output and assertion pass rates in every eval where a direct comparison exists, while without_skill, where it ran, was faster and cheaper, and in a minority of cases (2 of the 4 quality-compared evals) was favored on output quality. Nearly half of the evals lack without_skill data entirely, which limits how much can be concluded about without_skill's overall behavior from this run.


Note: a DevOps Agent endpoint outage failed some runs in this pass. Those scenarios (bc-iam-boundary, direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, invocation-log-destination-unprotected, kb-vector-index-deleted) were rerun on the same agent spaces with the same settings, and their results replace the failed runs.

access-denied-iam-vs-scp.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about distinguishing an IAM deny from an SCP (Service Control Policy) explicit deny. The trigger behavior fired as expected (1/1).

Expected output: Both with_skill and without_skill fully met the expected output criteria (1/1, 100%), with high-confidence judgments on both sides — this dimension shows no difference between them.

Assertions (5 total, each evaluated on a single run, so results should be read as single data points rather than stable rates):
- Three assertions passed for both variants (distinguishing IAM vs. SCP deny, naming a concrete way to tell them apart, considering model-access/marketplace-subscription causes, and no raw account ID exposure) — these did not differentiate the variants.
- One assertion (no raw 12-digit account ID exposed, regex-checked) also passed for both.
- One key assertion — that an SCP explicit deny cannot be overridden by account-level IAM and must be escalated to the Organizations administrator — passed for with_skill (1/1) but failed for without_skill (0/1), both with high confidence. This is the one substantive point of divergence in correctness/completeness between the two outputs.

Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 5/5 (100%), without_skill 4/5 (80%).

Quality comparison: Across the one pair evaluated, without_skill was favored over with_skill on all three judged criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with medium average confidence. This is based on only a single comparison pair, so it should be treated as a limited, low-volume signal rather than a robust pattern — and it stands somewhat in tension with the assertion results, where with_skill passed the SCP-escalation point that without_skill missed.

Metrics: with_skill took longer (24s vs 8s, ~16s more) and cost more ($0.20 vs $0.07) than without_skill, with somewhat higher context window utilization (7.6% vs 4.7%); neither variant triggered any context compaction or exceeded the runtime threshold.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (no data reported), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-run evaluation, so all findings are based on limited sample size. The one assertion failure for without_skill (missing the SCP-escalation guidance) is a concrete, high-confidence miss, while the quality-comparison result favoring without_skill conflicts with that assertion finding and rests on only one judged pair with medium confidence. Variant_a took noticeably longer and cost more than without_skill. No single dimension here provides a conclusive picture, and the mixed signals (assertion failure for without_skill vs. quality judges favoring without_skill) suggest the dimensions should be weighed together rather than treated as a consistent verdict.

In sum: for this single task, with_skill satisfied the expected output and more assertions (including a security-relevant one about account ID exposure), while without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper but failed the expected-output check and two assertions. This evaluation covers a single chat task testing how the agent diagnoses a Bedrock knowledge base failure (expected: identify it as an S3 permissions issue, name s3:GetObject and the service role, raise ticket code LLM-KB-011, and avoid leaking a raw account ID).

The behavior under test fired as expected (trigger_fired 1/1). From there, the two variants diverged sharply:

- with_skill met the expected output (1/1, high confidence) and passed all 5 assertions (5/5, 100%), including both LLM-judged assertions (correct classification as a permissions problem, correct naming of s3:GetObject/service role, raising LLM-KB-011 without modifying the role/policy) and both regex checks (mentions LLM-KB-011, no raw account ID exposed).
- without_skill did not meet the expected output (0/1, high confidence) and failed all 5 assertions (0/5, 0%) — the same three LLM-judged checks and two regex checks that with_skill passed.

This is a case where every single assertion shows the same with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, with high confidence on both sides, meaning the measurement is consistent and not an artifact of a shaky judge — though it's worth noting this is based on only one task instance, so it reflects this single scenario rather than broad behavioral evidence.

On efficiency metrics, without_skill was faster (24s vs 35s) and cheaper ($0.20 vs $0.29), with lower context utilization (4.3% vs 8.2%). Taken alone this would look like an efficiency advantage for without_skill, but since without_skill's output failed to meet the task's correctness requirements in this run, the lower cost/time came alongside a response that did not satisfy any of the defined checks — so this isn't a case of a favorable speed/quality tradeoff but rather a difference in outcome correctness that any time/cost savings don't offset on their own.

No quality comparison data is available (0 pairs evaluated, 1 pair skipped), and output consistency (run-to-run variation) was not measured for either variant (both null), so we cannot speak to how stable these results would be across repeated runs or corroborate the quality gap with pairwise judgment.

invocation-log-destination-unprotected.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task testing whether an agent correctly inspects a CloudWatch log group's encryption/retention settings and flags a specific finding (LLM-INV-010, severity HIGH).

Trigger and expected-output: The triggering behavior fired as expected, and both with_skill and without_skill met the overall "expected output" criterion in their single test run, with high-confidence judgments on both sides.

Assertions (per-assertion detail matters here, since the aggregate pass rate masks a split pattern): Of 5 assertions, 2 passed for both variants — correctly reading the log group's encryption/retention settings, and correctly stating there is no customer-managed KMS key with retention never expiring. These two are not differentiating since both variants handled them equally well. The remaining 3 assertions all passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill: raising the specific finding LLM-INV-010 with HIGH severity, naming LLM-INV-010 explicitly, and avoiding exposure of a raw 12-digit account ID. This produced an overall assertion pass rate of 5/5 (100%) for with_skill versus 2/5 (40%) for without_skill, driven entirely by this cluster of three related failures (likely reflecting a single underlying gap in without_skill's output — not naming/raising the finding, and incidentally exposing an account ID).

Quality comparison: Based on one evaluated pair (quality evaluated just once, so confidence in this comparison is limited), without_skill was favored in more cases (3) than with_skill (1), with 2 rated comparable, at medium average confidence. Looking at per-criterion breakdown: accuracy and completeness both favored without_skill over with_skill (with one comparable each), while actionability was split evenly (one favored each). This quality read is somewhat in tension with the assertion results, where with_skill passed the specific compliance-oriented checks (naming the finding, correct severity, not exposing account ID) that without_skill missed — suggesting the quality judgment may be weighing different aspects (e.g., narrative accuracy/completeness) than the strict assertions did.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took longer on average (31s vs 22s) and cost more ($0.26 vs $0.19). Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the single pair evaluated. Context window utilization was low for both (7.4% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (marked null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this evaluation.

Overall, this is a single-task evaluation with only one quality pair evaluated, so confidence in any broad conclusion is limited. The clearest, most concrete finding is the assertion split: with_skill reliably named and correctly raised the specific finding (LLM-INV-010, HIGH) and avoided exposing the account ID, while without_skill did not in this run. At the same time, a separate quality judgment (medium confidence, single pair) favored without_skill on accuracy and completeness, and without_skill ran faster and at lower cost. These are tradeoffs across different dimensions rather than one variant uniformly outperforming the other.
